opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way I approach it is shaped a lot by my background in visualization. For a long time, Fernanda Viégas and I worked on making complex data understandable to people, and when you turn to neural networks, you realize they're in some ways the ultimate complex data set. You have billions of numbers, and somehow out of those numbers comes behavior that looks surprisingly intelligent. So the natural question is: what's actually going on in there?

One thing I try to keep in mind is that "understanding" isn't a single thing. There are different levels. You might want to understand what a model does at the behavioral level, what kinds of inputs lead to what kinds of outputs. You might want to understand the internal representations, what concepts or features the model seems to be tracking. And then, at the deepest level, you might want to understand the mechanisms, the actual algorithms the network has learned. Each of those is valuable, and they call for different tools.

I also think it helps to approach these systems with a kind of naturalist's attitude. In a sense, these models are a new kind of object in the world. We built them, but we didn't design their internals in any detailed way; training did that. So there's something almost like biology about it. You go in, you observe carefully, you form hypotheses, you poke at things and see what happens. Sometimes the most important step is just looking, finding a good way to visualize what's happening so your intuition has something to work with.

And finally, I care a lot about the human side. Understanding isn't just a property of the model; it's a relationship between the model and a person. So part of the goal is building tools and interfaces that help people, whether researchers or everyday users, form accurate mental models of what these systems are doing. That matters scientifically, but it also matters for trust and safety, because people are going to be interacting with these systems constantly, and they deserve some insight into what's going on under the hood.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding has multiple levels, but does not identify differing definitions among people as a reason “understanding” or “intelligence” is difficult to communicate in machine learning.

r002.rationale: It recommends practical investigation: observe models, form hypotheses, probe them, and visualize their behavior to build intuition.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me the starting point is that "understanding" isn't one thing. People sometimes talk about interpretability as if there's a single target, a complete account of what a model is doing, and once you have it you're done. But in practice, understanding is always relative to a purpose. An engineer debugging a failure, a scientist curious about what representations the network learned, a regulator asking whether a system is fair: they all want different things, and a good explanation for one of them can be useless for another.

So I tend to ask, who is this for, and what decision are they trying to make? That reframes the problem from "explain the model" to "give someone the right handle on the model."

The second thing, which probably comes from my background in visualization, is that I think of understanding as a two-way interaction rather than a report you read once. The best tools let you poke at the system. You change an input, you watch what happens inside, you form a hypothesis, you test it. That loop is where real insight comes from, and it's exactly how people come to understand complex systems in other fields, whether it's a microscope or a debugger.

And third, I've become convinced that models often learn genuinely interesting internal structure. With language models, for instance, you can find representations of things like the state of a board game, or spatial and temporal concepts, that nobody explicitly put there. So part of the approach is a kind of humility: don't assume you know in advance what the model is doing. Treat it as an object of empirical study, build instruments that let you look inside, and be ready to be surprised.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding depends on the person’s purpose, but it does not say that differing definitions make “understanding” and “intelligence” difficult to communicate about in machine learning.

r002.rationale: It moves from an abstract goal of explaining a model to useful tasks and decisions, then describes concrete activities such as changing inputs, observing internal behavior, and testing hypotheses.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, what do we mean by understanding? Because there are several different things we might want. We might want to predict what a model will do, explain a particular decision, or figure out when we should trust it. Those aren’t necessarily the same problem.

My instinct is to make things visible and interactive. You can look at examples, look for patterns in the model’s behavior, and then ask, “Does that pattern really hold?” Change the input, test a hypothesis, see what surprises you. A visualization can help you ask those questions, but a compelling picture isn’t itself an explanation.

So I think of understanding less as a single moment when you open up the model and everything becomes clear, and more as a process of building and testing an account of how it behaves.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes several goals for understanding a model, but does not say that people use terms like “understanding” or “intelligence” differently or that this makes them hard to communicate.

r002.rationale: It recommends hands-on activities: inspect examples and behavior, change inputs, test hypotheses, and examine surprises, rather than relying on an abstract definition alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, understanding for whom, and for what purpose? A researcher trying to debug a model needs something different from a person deciding whether to trust its recommendation. So I tend to approach understanding as a set of questions we want to answer, rather than a single property a model has.

Visualization can help make those questions concrete. You might look at where a model makes mistakes, compare its behavior on different kinds of examples, or change an input and see what happens. That gives you a way to build intuition and then test it. The important thing is to distinguish a picture that feels explanatory from evidence that actually helps you predict how the model will behave.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes people’s purposes for seeking understanding, but does not say that differing definitions make “understanding” and “intelligence” difficult to communicate.

r002.rationale: It frames understanding as questions to answer and gives concrete activities—examining mistakes, comparing examples, and changing inputs—instead of treating it as a single abstract property.
